what: The board moved against us within half an hour of our uploads. Rank sum is 86, not 84.

tier3-auc.cause: maniphys.ai went 0.22590 -> 0.28173 at 2026-10-29 21:43, 27 minutes after our 21:16 upload

tier3-mppe.cause: maniphys.ai went 49.93762 -> 36.60061 at 21:44, so the position we took from them at 21:17 was taken back in 27 minutes

tier1-auc.cause: Izus_systems reached 0.82849 at 21:45; our rank is unchanged but the field grew

what_i_had_been_reporting: 84, correct at 21:17 and stale by 21:44. I carried it forward for several hours without re-checking, which is exactly the kind of number that should be re-measured rather than remembered.
the_strategic_point: This is the most decision-relevant thing measured today. The board is NOT static: at least two teams uploaded improvements in the same hours we did, and one of them erased both of our rank gains within half an hour. Three consequences. First, holding credit has a cost -- a gain banked today can be overtaken tomorrow, so spending on the best available arm sooner is better than waiting for a better arm. Second, the gaps quoted in docs/TO_THE_TOP.md are a snapshot and will have moved by the time any arm finishes. Third, maniphys.ai's Tier 3 jump (AUC +0.056, MPPE -13.3 cm in one upload) is larger than anything our fine-tune arm produced, which suggests they changed method rather than selection -- most plausibly a better reconstruction, which is exactly what our own headroom analysis says binds Tier 3 (eleven clips where the policy already beats its input).
what_it_does_not_change: Our own numbers are unchanged and still verified: Tier 1 0.52687, Tier 2 0.46522, Tier 3 0.26781 / 0.20000 / 47.77180. We lost rank to someone else's improvement, not to a regression of ours.

the_obvious_response_and_why_it_is_block.idea: If maniphys.ai's Tier 3 jump came from a better reconstruction, the cheap analogue for us is to CLEAN our existing reconstruction rather than redo it: we already have a support-surface cleaner (built for Tier 2, 0.4247 -> 0.4755 on that tier) and the released support primitives are already in use on Tier 3 via scene.support per clip, so applying the cleaner to the reconstruction is legal and free CPU.
the_obvious_response_and_why_it_is_block.why_it_does_not_help_the_current_entry: Our submitted rollouts were produced by policies driven by the UNCLEANED reconstruction. Cleaning the reference now changes no rollout. To benefit we would have to re-drive the policies with the cleaned reference, and that is the cold-swap experiment we already ran on Tier 1: substituting a cleaner reference under a policy trained on a different one took the entry from 0.46523 to 0.28937, because each actor learned one specific trajectory. So the predictable outcome is worse, not better.
the_obvious_response_and_why_it_is_block.what_would_actually_be_needed: Clean the reconstruction AND retrain on it -- reference change plus 350M steps per clip, about $90 for 30 clips. That is the same price as the checkpoint-selection arm and for the same reason: anything that changes the reference requires refitting the policy to it. The warm-start finding says exactly this: gains come from re-fitting to a NEW reference, never from swapping one under a finished policy.
the_obvious_response_and_why_it_is_block.the_one_thing_worth_doing_free: Measure how much the cleaner would lower the reconstruction floor, which is pure CPU and tells us whether a funded reconstruction arm is worth $90 before anyone pays for it. Our floors run to 271 cm on e19 and 212 on e27; if the cleaner takes the worst of them to 20-40 cm the arm is compelling, and if it barely moves them the binding constraint is the reconstruction method itself and no amount of cleaning helps.
